rows.caution: A reader should not conclude that stacking these two routes yields a confirmed mechanism whereby sustained NO release (rather than early burst release, or BVLD acting alone/synergistically, or a general anti-fouling surface property) causes the lower platelet adhesion, activation, and thrombosis. Route B's concordant ranking is a correlation across only 5 surface-level points and does not test causality or timing; Route A's release-duration argument is a candidate explanation not verified by any time-matched assay. The two routes also share, rather than independently overcome, the same BVLD/NO confound, so they should not be read as independent lines of corroboration for the specific NO-release-duration mechanism -- only as jointly consistent with a broader, less specific antithrombotic effect of the modified surfaces.

A reader should not treat the two routes as independent corroboration that strengthens the causal case for NO release reducing thrombosis -- they draw on the same underlying experiment and same five surfaces, and both are compromised by the identical unresolved confound (BVLD, an anticoagulant, is present only in the two best-performing surfaces, one of which also has NO). Route B in particular adds little beyond restating that two outcome metrics agree with each other, which is close to tautological. Neither route establishes a dose/time-response relationship between NO release duration and anti-thrombotic performance, nor isolates NO's contribution from BVLD's. Two weak, overlapping, associative routes do not sum to a causal or mechanistic conclusion; the combined evidence remains descriptive/associative at best.

A reader should not treat Route B as a second, independent line of evidence for the YS-vs-creep divergence claim, since it never discusses creep and cannot rule out that dispersion appearance is just tracking particle amount rather than a distinct microstructural effect. A reader should also not read Route A's qualitative curve-position language (below/overlap/above AZ91) as a quantified measure of how much creep resistance improved, nor assume the YS and creep measurements were taken under comparable test conditions. Two routes that each carry acknowledged qualitative, unquantified, potentially confounded limits do not sum to strong or mechanistic support for claim n13; at most they yield a plausible, non-contradicted, but still associative and partly-covered picture of composition-dependent mechanical trade-offs.

A reader should not treat the pairing of two disjoint-evidence routes as strengthening the case for a mechanistic claim about n13 into something causal or discriminating. Each route already relies on an inference its own evidence does not fully cover (A: assumed identity of macro 'deformation bands' with the microscopically defined wavy bands, and no direct temperature series for the wavy-band feature itself; B: correlation-not-causation on a single specimen with no temperature attribution). Combining two such partly-warranted, non-overlapping routes does not make the underlying claim about n13 well established -- it broadens the topics touched (band persistence vs. basal-slip ductility) without cross-checking or reinforcing either inference, and should not be read as convergent independent confirmation of one specific mechanism.

A reader should not treat the two routes as two fully independent lines of evidence converging on the same conclusion; because both rely on the same EBSD orientation-map observation as a common anchor, part of the apparent agreement reflects shared data rather than separate corroboration. Neither route provides a quantitative, matrix-calibrated misorientation measurement, and neither route provides SAED (or any diffraction-based point measurement) on the twin bands themselves — the claim that twin bands are internally uniform rests only on EBSD/OM appearance in both routes, never on an independent quantitative check. The combination should be read as a corroborated qualitative/associative characterization of band type versus orientation behaviour, not as a mechanistic explanation of why kink bands develop continuously varying orientation, nor as a discriminating test that rules out alternative causes of the EBSD shading (e.g., diffraction-contrast artifacts, given that OM and EBSD contrast arise from different physical mechanisms).
